quests.instruction: Build this paragraph so the explanation clarifies the support rather than repeating the claim.
quests.essayTopic: Explain why labelling emotions can help someone manage them
options: Naming an emotion out loud can make it easier to manage.
The label does not remove the feeling, but it gives the mind something to hold onto besides the feeling itself.
People who say 'I feel anxious' rather than simply feeling anxious often calm down within minutes.
Putting a feeling into words engages a part of the brain associated with reasoning, which quiets the part driving the raw reaction.
quests.hint: The explanation should say why the support happens, not just restate that it does. Check which sentence adds a reason rather than another fact.
quests.explanation: The claim states the position. The support shows the pattern occurring in people, which the explanation then accounts for by describing the underlying mechanism. The closing insight reflects on what that mechanism actually achieves, which is why it comes last.
quests.thesisStatement: Naming an emotion out loud can make it noticeably easier to manage.

quests.instruction: Order this paragraph so the specific detail comes only after the reader knows what general point it supports.
quests.essayTopic: Explain why handwritten notes can help some students remember material better than typed notes
options: Writing notes by hand can help some students remember material better than typing does.
A student who writes 'cause: pressure drop' instead of copying a full sentence has already done some of the thinking typing would postpone.
Handwriting is slower than typing, which forces a student to summarise an idea instead of copying it word for word.
The slower method, in this case, is doing more mental work along the way.
quests.hint: The specific detail is an example of the mechanism, so it needs the mechanism explained before it can be understood as an example of anything.
quests.explanation: The claim states the position. The explanation gives the general mechanism, summarising versus copying, which the specific detail then illustrates concretely. The closing insight draws the point together once the illustration has made it vivid.
quests.thesisStatement: Writing notes by hand can help some students remember material better than typing does.

quests.instruction: Arrange this paragraph so the reader understands why the example matters before being shown its conclusion.
quests.essayTopic: Explain why explaining a concept aloud reveals gaps in understanding
options: A student confident about photosynthesis may freeze halfway through explaining it aloud, realising they never understood how the steps connect.
The freeze is not a failure so much as useful information about what still needs work.
Speaking requires organising an idea into a clear sequence, which is harder to fake than simply recognising the idea on a page.
Explaining an idea aloud to someone else often reveals gaps that silent reading hides.
quests.hint: The example should demonstrate the mechanism, which means the mechanism has to be described first for the example to make sense as an example.
quests.explanation: The claim states the position. The explanation gives the reason speaking is harder to fake than reading, and the example shows that difficulty happening to a real student. The closing insight reframes the moment positively, which only works once the reader has seen it happen.
quests.thesisStatement: Explaining an idea aloud often reveals gaps in understanding that silent reading hides.

quests.instruction: Choose the arrangement where the specific example does real work, not just decoration, and order the paragraph.
quests.essayTopic: Explain why clear labelling in a grocery store affects what customers buy
options: Customers, it turns out, are choosing based on how easily a product explains itself, not only on what is actually inside the box.
Clear labelling in a grocery store quietly shapes what customers end up buying.
Products placed at eye level with bold, simple labels tend to outsell similar products just a shelf away.
A cereal box redesigned with larger, plainer text saw sales rise even though the recipe inside stayed exactly the same.
quests.hint: A vague example would only restate the pattern. Find the one with a specific, concrete detail that proves the pattern is real.
quests.explanation: The claim states the position. The general pattern describes the trend across products, and the specific example grounds it in one concrete, verifiable case. The consequence closes by interpreting what that case reveals about customer behaviour.
quests.thesisStatement: Clear labelling in a grocery store quietly shapes what customers end up buying, sometimes more than the product itself does.

quests.instruction: This paragraph needs a concrete detail, not a vague restatement. Order it so the specific case earns its place.
quests.essayTopic: Explain why small acts of recognition improve morale at work
options: A manager who mentions, in a team meeting, exactly which part of a report was well done gives an employee something a general bonus never provides: proof that the work was actually noticed.
Small, specific acts of recognition do more for workplace morale than large, occasional rewards.
It is the noticing, more than the reward itself, that seems to matter most.
Employees who receive brief, regular acknowledgement of their work tend to report higher satisfaction than those waiting for an annual bonus.
quests.hint: Compare the general sentence with the concrete one. The concrete one should name a specific behaviour, not just say 'recognition helps.'
quests.explanation: The claim states the position. The general pattern describes the trend, and the specific example illustrates it through a precise, observable action, a manager naming exactly what was done well. The insight closes by drawing out what that concrete detail reveals.
quests.thesisStatement: Small, specific acts of recognition do more for workplace morale than large, occasional rewards.

quests.instruction: Order this paragraph so a genuinely specific case follows and supports the general claim, rather than merely repeating it.
quests.essayTopic: Explain why simplifying a form can increase how many people complete it
options: Reducing the number of questions on a form can significantly increase how many people finish filling it out.
One charity cut its donation form from eleven fields to four and saw completed donations rise by nearly a third within a month.
Long forms tend to lose a portion of users at every additional field they are asked to complete.
Each removed question, it seems, removes one more chance for a visitor to give up.
quests.hint: The specific case should be a single, real, measurable instance. Place it after the general pattern it is meant to prove.
quests.explanation: The claim states the position. The general pattern describes the trend across forms broadly, and the specific case grounds that trend in one measurable, real example. The closing insight interprets what that example demonstrates about each question's cost.
quests.thesisStatement: Reducing the number of questions on a form can significantly increase how many people finish filling it out.

quests.instruction: This paragraph should deepen its point across four sentences, not restate it. Order it so each sentence adds something new.
quests.essayTopic: Explain why a good mentor asks questions rather than giving direct answers
options: A good mentor often helps more by asking questions than by handing over direct answers.
A well-placed question forces the mentee to reason through the problem themselves, building a method they can reuse without the mentor present.
Over time, the mentee needs the mentor less, which is the actual measure of the mentoring having worked.
A direct answer solves today's problem but teaches nothing about solving tomorrow's.
quests.hint: Each sentence should go one layer deeper than the last: from the immediate cost, to what questions build instead, to the eventual payoff.
quests.explanation: The claim states the position. The first layer explains what direct answers fail to build, and the deeper layer explains what questions build instead, extending rather than repeating the first layer. The result closes by naming the long-term payoff, which depends on both layers already being explained.
quests.thesisStatement: A good mentor often helps more by asking questions than by handing over direct answers.

quests.instruction: Elaborate rather than repeat: order this paragraph so each sentence adds a new layer of reasoning.
quests.essayTopic: Explain why admitting a mistake quickly tends to preserve trust better than hiding it
options: That reputation for honesty ends up mattering more, over years, than any single mistake ever does.
An early admission gives the people affected time to adjust before the mistake grows into a bigger problem.
Admitting a mistake quickly tends to preserve trust better than trying to hide it.
It also signals that the person can be relied on to tell the truth even when the truth is uncomfortable.
quests.hint: The immediate effect and the deeper effect should not be two versions of the same idea. One is practical, the other is about reputation.
quests.explanation: The claim states the position. The immediate effect addresses the practical benefit of early warning, and the deeper effect extends the reasoning to reputation, a genuinely different layer. The long-term result closes by projecting that reputation forward.
quests.thesisStatement: Admitting a mistake quickly tends to preserve trust better than trying to hide it.

quests.instruction: Order this paragraph so the reasoning develops through genuinely different layers rather than circling the same point.
quests.essayTopic: Explain why setting a specific number, rather than a vague goal, improves the odds of following through
options: A number like 'save fifty pounds a month' removes both problems at once, giving progress something visible to measure against.
A specific number attached to a goal improves the odds of actually following through on it.
A vague goal also gives the mind an easy excuse to quietly lower its own standard without ever noticing it has done so.
'Save some money' gives no way to tell, on any given day, whether progress is being made.
quests.hint: Look for two layers that are genuinely different: one about measurable progress, one about how the mind quietly excuses itself.
quests.explanation: The claim states the position. The practical layer addresses measurability, and the psychological layer extends the reasoning into a different territory, how vagueness enables self-deception. The result closes by showing how a specific number solves both layers at once.
quests.thesisStatement: A specific number attached to a goal improves the odds of actually following through on it.

quests.instruction: Order this paragraph so the reader understands why this particular evidence was chosen, not just what it shows.
quests.essayTopic: Explain why customer testimonials can be more persuasive than product specifications
options: Buyers, in the end, are trying to picture a future, not evaluate a spec sheet.
Specifications describe the product; a testimonial describes the experience of owning it, which is closer to what the buyer is actually imagining.
A short customer testimonial can persuade a buyer more effectively than a page of technical specifications.
A review describing how a backpack survived three years of daily commuting says more to most buyers than a listing of denier and stitch count.
quests.hint: Distinguish the sentence that simply presents the evidence from the one that explains why that particular kind of evidence carries weight.
quests.explanation: The claim states the position. The evidence gives a concrete comparison, and the sentence explaining why this evidence matters clarifies the deeper reason it persuades, that it maps onto imagined experience rather than technical fact. The closing insight generalises from that reason.
quests.thesisStatement: A short customer testimonial can persuade a buyer more effectively than a page of technical specifications.

quests.instruction: Arrange this paragraph so the reason the evidence is convincing is explained, not assumed.
quests.essayTopic: Explain why a before-and-after comparison is convincing evidence in a renovation advertisement
options: Placed side by side, a cluttered, dated kitchen and its bright, updated replacement need no caption to make their point.
A before-and-after photograph is one of the most persuasive tools a renovation company can use.
A claim that would otherwise need pages of description is settled in a single glance.
The comparison persuades because it removes the buyer's need to imagine the result; the eyes do the work argument usually has to do.
quests.hint: Look for the sentence that explains what makes this specific kind of evidence work, rather than the sentence that just describes it.
quests.explanation: The claim states the position. The evidence describes the specific comparison, and the sentence explaining why it persuades identifies the underlying reason, removing the need for imagination. The closing insight restates the efficiency of that persuasion.
quests.thesisStatement: A before-and-after photograph is one of the most persuasive tools a renovation company can use.

quests.instruction: Order this paragraph so the reader learns why the chosen evidence is stronger than an alternative would have been.
quests.essayTopic: Explain why a case study can be more convincing than a general statistic in a business proposal
options: A statistic like 'most companies see improvement' invites doubt about whether this company counts as 'most,' while a detailed case study answers that doubt directly.
Specificity, in this sense, closes a gap that a general number leaves wide open.
A proposal describing exactly how one similar company cut costs by twenty percent, and how, gives a client something to picture happening to their own business.
A single detailed case study can persuade a sceptical client more effectively than a broad statistic.
quests.hint: The sentence explaining the comparison should clarify exactly what the general statistic fails to do that the case study achieves.
quests.explanation: The claim states the position. The evidence gives the concrete case, and the comparison sentence explains precisely why a general statistic would leave doubt the case study removes. The closing insight names the underlying principle, specificity closing gaps.
quests.thesisStatement: A single detailed case study can persuade a sceptical client more effectively than a broad statistic.

quests.instruction: Order this paragraph so the claim is followed by real support rather than another unsupported assertion.
quests.essayTopic: Explain why frequent short breaks help maintain focus during long tasks
options: A short pause, then, is not lost time but a way of protecting the time that follows it.
Attention naturally drifts after sustained effort, and a brief pause appears to reset it rather than simply delaying tiredness.
Workers given a five-minute break each hour completed a proofreading task with fewer missed errors than workers who worked straight through.
Taking short breaks every hour helps maintain focus during long, demanding tasks.
quests.hint: Every claim in a strong paragraph needs a sentence that could convince a skeptic. Check which sentence actually provides that kind of proof.
quests.explanation: The claim states the position. The support gives a concrete comparison a reader could verify, and the explanation accounts for why that comparison came out the way it did. The closing insight reframes the finding, which depends on the support and explanation already being established.
quests.thesisStatement: Taking short breaks every hour helps maintain focus during long, demanding tasks.

quests.instruction: This paragraph should build a case a skeptical reader could accept. Order it so real support precedes the interpretation.
quests.essayTopic: Explain why offering a free trial period can increase a subscription service's long-term customers
options: Offering a free trial period can increase the number of long-term customers a subscription service keeps.
Services that switched from a discounted first month to a genuinely free trial reported higher conversion to paying subscribers over the following year.
A free trial removes the small financial risk that otherwise stops hesitant users from ever trying the product at all.
Once a habit forms during the trial, cancelling starts to feel like a loss rather than simply avoiding a cost.
quests.hint: Distinguish the sentence that gives a skeptic something to check from the sentence that only explains a mechanism without evidence behind it.
quests.explanation: The claim states the position. The support provides a comparison a reader could investigate, and the explanation accounts for the psychological reason behind that comparison. The closing insight extends the explanation into what happens once the trial ends.
quests.thesisStatement: Offering a free trial period can increase the number of long-term customers a subscription service keeps.

quests.instruction: Order this paragraph so a claim about behaviour is backed by an observable case rather than asserted alone.
quests.essayTopic: Explain why displaying calorie counts on a menu can change what customers order
options: Displaying calorie counts on a menu can quietly change what customers choose to order.
Restaurants that added calorie labels saw average order sizes shrink slightly, even though most customers said the numbers did not influence them.
The influence, in other words, may work below the level customers are even aware of.
Seeing a specific number attached to a dish seems to trigger a small, mostly unconscious moment of reconsideration.
quests.hint: The support should be something a reader could verify or imagine verifying, not just a restatement of the claim in different words.
quests.explanation: The claim states the position. The support offers a real, checkable outcome, and the explanation accounts for why the outcome occurred despite customers denying influence. The closing insight interprets that gap between belief and behaviour, which needs both prior sentences established.
quests.thesisStatement: Displaying calorie counts on a menu can quietly change what customers choose to order.

quests.instruction: Two sentences look similar but serve different jobs: one is evidence, one explains it. Place them correctly.
quests.essayTopic: Explain why decluttering a workspace can improve concentration
options: The eyes, it turns out, are as easily distracted as the ears.
A tidy workspace can measurably improve how well someone concentrates.
Office workers moved to a decluttered desk completed a focus-based task faster than those left at a cluttered one.
Visual clutter competes for attention the same way a noisy room does, quietly pulling focus away from the task itself.
quests.hint: One sentence reports what happened; the other explains why it happened. Find which is which before ordering the paragraph.
quests.explanation: The claim states the position. The evidence reports an observed outcome, and the explanation accounts for the mechanism behind that outcome, which is why it follows rather than precedes the evidence. The closing insight draws a broader comparison from the explanation.
quests.thesisStatement: A tidy workspace can measurably improve how well someone concentrates.

quests.instruction: Separate the reported fact from the reasoning behind it, then order this paragraph correctly.
quests.essayTopic: Explain why students who explain material to a study partner tend to retain it longer
options: Teaching requires organising information clearly enough for someone else to follow, which forces a deeper level of processing than silent review does.
In one classroom comparison, students who taught a concept to a partner scored higher on a test a month later than students who had simply reread the same material.
Students who explain material to a study partner tend to remember it longer than those who only review it silently.
The partner, in this sense, is almost incidental; the real benefit comes from the act of explaining itself.
quests.hint: Check which sentence a skeptic could verify with a test score, and which sentence only makes sense as an account of why that score happened.
quests.explanation: The claim states the position. The evidence reports a verifiable comparison, and the explanation accounts for why teaching produces that result. The closing insight interprets the explanation further, which is why it comes last.
quests.thesisStatement: Students who explain material to a study partner tend to remember it longer than those who only review it silently.

quests.instruction: This paragraph mixes a reported outcome with the reasoning behind it. Untangle and order them correctly.
quests.essayTopic: Explain why writing down a worry before bed can reduce how much it disrupts sleep
options: The list, in effect, gives the mind permission to stop rehearsing what it has already written down.
Writing down a worry before bed can reduce how much it disrupts sleep later that night.
Writing the worry down seems to signal to the mind that it has been recorded and no longer needs to be actively held onto.
People who wrote a short list of tomorrow's tasks before bed fell asleep faster, on average, than people who did not.
quests.hint: One sentence is a measurable result; the other is a proposed reason for that result. The reason should follow the result it is explaining.
quests.explanation: The claim states the position. The evidence reports a measurable outcome across two groups, and the explanation proposes the psychological reason behind that outcome. The closing insight restates the explanation memorably, which depends on it already being introduced.
quests.thesisStatement: Writing down a worry before bed can reduce how much it disrupts sleep later that night.

quests.instruction: This paragraph blends a specific example with a general mechanism. Order it so both are placed where they do the most work.
quests.essayTopic: Explain why gradual exposure helps someone overcome a specific fear
options: Someone afraid of public speaking might start by speaking to one trusted friend, then a small group, before addressing a room of strangers.
By the time the larger step arrives, the body has already learned, in smaller doses, that it can handle it.
Facing a fear in small, manageable steps tends to work better than avoiding it or confronting it all at once.
Each small step teaches the nervous system that the feared situation is survivable, slightly lowering the alarm response before the next step.
quests.hint: The mechanism should be understood before the specific example, since the example is a case of the mechanism at work.
quests.explanation: The claim states the position. The mechanism explains the general process, and the concrete example shows that process happening in a specific, relatable situation. The synthesis closes by connecting the example back to the mechanism explicitly.
quests.thesisStatement: Facing a fear in small, manageable steps tends to work better than avoiding it or confronting it all at once.

quests.instruction: Order this paragraph so the general reasoning and the specific case each do a distinct job in the right sequence.
quests.essayTopic: Explain why spacing out study sessions works better than cramming
options: Revisiting material after a delay forces the brain to retrieve it rather than simply recognise it, which strengthens the memory more.
A student who reviews vocabulary on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday tends to recall more of it a month later than a student who reviewed it all in one long Sunday session.
Spreading study sessions across several days works better than cramming the night before.
The gaps between sessions, uncomfortable as they can feel, are doing real work.
quests.hint: The mechanism explains the underlying reason; the concrete example shows it happening to a specific student. Order them so the reason comes first.
quests.explanation: The claim states the position. The mechanism explains the memory process involved, and the concrete example illustrates that process with a specific comparison. The synthesis closes by reframing the discomfort of spacing as productive, which depends on the mechanism already being clear.
quests.thesisStatement: Spreading study sessions across several days works better than cramming the night before.

quests.instruction: Arrange this paragraph so a general principle and a specific case build toward a single, earned synthesis.
quests.essayTopic: Explain why public commitment can increase the odds of following through on a goal
options: Someone who tells three friends they are training for a race is more likely to keep training than someone quietly hoping to.
A stated commitment creates a mild social cost for quitting, which private goals do not carry.
The friends do not need to check in for the effect to work; simply knowing they might is often enough.
Telling other people about a goal can increase the odds of actually following through on it.
quests.hint: The general principle about social cost should be understood before the specific example of the three friends can be recognised as an instance of it.
quests.explanation: The claim states the position. The mechanism names the underlying social cost involved, and the concrete example shows that cost operating in a specific, everyday situation. The synthesis closes by extending the explanation with a further nuance.
quests.thesisStatement: Telling other people about a goal can increase the odds of actually following through on it.

quests.instruction: This paragraph's evidence partly complicates the claim. Order it so the complication is handled honestly.
quests.essayTopic: Explain whether multitasking actually saves time
options: Switching between two tasks lets a person feel busy without ever leaving either task idle for long.
The feeling of productivity, in this case, is measuring something different from the actual result.
Multitasking feels efficient, but it rarely saves as much time as it seems to.
Studies measuring actual completion times, however, show that switching costs add up, often making both tasks take longer than doing them one at a time.
quests.hint: The complicating evidence should follow the evidence it complicates, not replace or precede it, so the contrast is clear.
quests.explanation: The claim states a position that anticipates complexity. The supporting evidence shows why multitasking feels efficient, which the complicating evidence then challenges with a measured cost. The balanced conclusion closes by naming the gap between feeling and reality.
quests.thesisStatement: Multitasking feels efficient, but it rarely saves as much time as it seems to.

quests.instruction: Order this paragraph so evidence that softens the claim appears only after the claim's initial support has been given fairly.
quests.essayTopic: Explain whether working from home increases employee productivity
options: Working from home tends to increase productivity, though the effect depends heavily on the type of work involved.
The real answer, then, depends less on the location than on how much a role relies on unplanned interaction.

Employees whose work depends on quick, spontaneous collaboration, however, sometimes report the opposite, since useful conversations that once happened by chance now require deliberate effort to arrange.
Employees doing focused, independent tasks often report completing more in a home environment free of office interruptions.
quests.hint: The softening evidence should follow the initial support, creating a fair contrast rather than contradicting the claim outright.
quests.explanation: The claim opens with a qualified position. The supporting evidence backs the general trend, and the softening evidence complicates it for a specific kind of role. The balanced conclusion closes by identifying the real variable behind both outcomes.
quests.thesisStatement: Working from home tends to increase productivity, though the effect depends heavily on the type of work involved.

quests.instruction: Arrange this paragraph so the reader sees the claim genuinely tested by evidence on both sides before the conclusion.
quests.essayTopic: Explain whether standardised testing accurately measures student ability
options: A single score, then, is accurate about a narrow slice of ability and silent about the rest.
Tests are consistent enough that two students with similar knowledge tend to receive similar scores, which is exactly what a fair measurement should do.
They struggle, however, to capture creativity, persistence, or the ability to work well with others, qualities that matter just as much outside an exam hall.
Standardised tests measure some abilities reliably, but not the full range of what makes a student capable.
quests.hint: The complicating evidence should genuinely test the claim rather than simply repeating the support. Place it after the support it complicates.
quests.explanation: The claim opens by acknowledging both a strength and a limit. The supporting evidence explains what tests do measure well, and the complicating evidence explains what they miss, creating a genuine contrast. The balanced conclusion closes by naming the overall shape of that limitation.
quests.thesisStatement: Standardised tests measure some abilities reliably, but not the full range of what makes a student capable.

quests.instruction: One sentence looks like an explanation but is actually just the evidence restated. Identify the real explanation and order the paragraph.
quests.essayTopic: Explain why offering fewer choices can make a decision easier for a customer
options: A jam stall offering six flavours sold more jars than the same stall offering twenty-four flavours, even though more people stopped to look at the larger display.
Too many options make each one harder to evaluate against the others, so the effort of comparing can outweigh the desire to choose at all.
Fewer choices, paradoxically, can feel more generous than a wall of options ever does.
Offering fewer options can make it easier for a customer to actually decide and buy something.
quests.hint: Check whether a candidate sentence explains why the pattern happens, or just restates that it happens in different words.
quests.explanation: The claim states the position. The evidence reports the jam stall comparison, and the real explanation accounts for the psychological reason behind that comparison, the cost of evaluating too many options. The closing insight reflects on the paradox, which depends on the explanation already being given.
quests.thesisStatement: Offering fewer options can make it easier for a customer to actually decide and buy something.

quests.instruction: Distinguish a genuine explanation from a sentence that only rephrases the evidence, then order this paragraph.
quests.essayTopic: Explain why removing a countdown timer can reduce anxiety while completing an online test
options: Removing a visible countdown timer can reduce anxiety while a student completes an online test.
Students given the same test without a visible timer reported feeling calmer and made fewer careless errors than students who could see time running out.
The time pressure was still there either way; only the awareness of it had changed.
A constantly visible countdown keeps part of the mind monitoring the clock instead of the question, splitting attention that a hidden timer leaves intact.
quests.hint: One sentence merely restates that students felt calmer; the other explains the mental mechanism behind that calm. Place the mechanism after the evidence.
quests.explanation: The claim states the position. The evidence reports the comparison between groups, and the real explanation accounts for why removing the timer changed the outcome, describing divided attention. The closing insight sharpens the point, which depends on the explanation already existing.
quests.thesisStatement: Removing a visible countdown timer can reduce anxiety while a student completes an online test.

quests.instruction: This paragraph contains a sentence that sounds explanatory but is only a rephrased fact. Find the true explanation and order accordingly.
quests.essayTopic: Explain why a default option on a form strongly influences what people choose
options: The option already selected by default on a form strongly influences what people end up choosing.
The form, in effect, made a choice for people who never quite got around to making one themselves.
Changing a default requires an active decision, and many people follow the path of least resistance rather than stopping to evaluate every option deliberately.
When a donation form defaulted to a monthly gift instead of a one-time gift, far more donors ended up giving monthly.
quests.hint: The real explanation should describe why people behave this way, not simply describe the outcome again using different words.
quests.explanation: The claim states the position. The evidence reports the donation form comparison, and the real explanation accounts for the behavioural tendency behind it, the path of least resistance. The closing insight restates that tendency vividly, which depends on the explanation already being clear.
quests.thesisStatement: The option already selected by default on a form strongly influences what people end up choosing.

quests.instruction: Full capstone: build a paragraph with a claim, layered explanation, real evidence, and a conclusion that reflects the evidence's actual weight.
quests.essayTopic: Explain whether financial incentives improve long-term employee performance
options: A bonus focuses attention sharply on whatever is being measured, sometimes at the expense of other parts of the job that matter just as much.
Financial incentives can improve performance in the short term, but their long-term effect is far less certain.
Sales teams offered a short-term bonus for closing more deals often saw a temporary spike in sales, followed by a return to previous levels once the bonus period ended.
The incentive changed behaviour temporarily without changing the underlying motivation that would have sustained the improvement.
quests.hint: This paragraph should chain every skill from this file: a claim honest about its own limits, a reason before the evidence, and a conclusion that matches what the evidence actually shows.
quests.explanation: The claim opens with a deliberately qualified position. The layered explanation gives the mechanism before the evidence, preparing the reader to interpret the sales-team result correctly. The careful conclusion closes by matching the claim's original caution, rather than overstating what a temporary spike actually proves.
quests.thesisStatement: Financial incentives can improve performance in the short term, but their long-term effect is far less certain.

quests.instruction: Capstone paragraph: integrate a mechanism, a concrete case, and evidence that complicates a simple version of the claim.
quests.essayTopic: Explain whether praising a child's intelligence helps or harms their motivation
options: A child praised for being smart may start associating their worth with always succeeding, rather than with the effort of trying.
Yet the same research shows that praising effort rather than intelligence produces the opposite result, with children choosing harder challenges more readily.
A student told 'you're so clever' after an easy test later avoided a harder one, worried that struggling would contradict the label.
Praising a child's intelligence can quietly harm their motivation, even though it is meant to encourage them.
quests.hint: The complicating evidence should offer a genuine contrast, showing what happens when the type of praise changes, not simply restate the original claim.
quests.explanation: The claim opens with a position that already anticipates nuance. The mechanism explains the psychological process, and the concrete case shows it happening to a real student. The complicating evidence closes by showing the reverse outcome under different conditions, deepening rather than repeating the claim.
quests.thesisStatement: Praising a child's intelligence can quietly harm their motivation, even though it is meant to encourage them.

quests.instruction: Final capstone of this file: assemble a paragraph that distinguishes evidence from explanation, elaborates in layers, and reaches a conclusion proportionate to the evidence.
quests.essayTopic: Explain whether reading a summary of a book provides the same benefit as reading the book itself
options: Readers who read only a summary of a nonfiction book performed worse on questions requiring them to apply an idea to a new situation than readers who read the full text.
A summary can convey a book's key ideas, but it rarely provides the same benefit as reading the book itself.
A full book gives ideas room to develop through examples, contradictions, and second thoughts that a summary has to strip away to stay short.
The summary preserved the facts of the book but not the practice of thinking through them that the full text demanded.
quests.hint: The conclusion should match exactly what the evidence tested, application rather than recall, rather than making a broader claim than the evidence supports.
quests.explanation: The claim opens with a qualified position. The explanation describes what a summary strips away, preparing the reader to interpret the evidence about application correctly. The proportionate conclusion closes by matching its claim precisely to what was tested, avoiding a broader claim than the evidence earns.
quests.thesisStatement: A summary can convey a book's key ideas, but it rarely provides the same benefit as reading the book itself.
